facts.text: Dengue is caused by a virus that Aedes mosquitoes pass to people: a mosquito that bites an infected person can later infect others when it bites them. Aedes aegypti is the main carrier; Aedes albopictus can also spread it.
Most people who catch dengue have mild symptoms or none at all, but some develop severe dengue.
There is no specific medicine that treats dengue.
A 2018 review of about 20 years of Taiwan CDC data found that more than 98% of local dengue cases in outbreaks were reported in southern Taiwan, mainly Tainan, Kaohsiung and Pingtung.

Aedes aegypti is found in southern Taiwan but appears to be absent from the north, while Aedes albopictus lives across the island. The author suggests Aedes aegypti cannot survive the cold, wet winters of northern Taiwan.

Aedes aegypti prefers to stay indoors and mainly bites humans, while Aedes albopictus prefers to stay outdoors and mainly bites animals; this is why Aedes aegypti is the main dengue carrier in Taiwan.
Female Aedes mosquitoes lay their eggs on the inner walls of containers that hold water, just above the waterline, for example buckets, vases, flowerpot saucers, barrels and tires.
The eggs hatch when water, such as rain, rises and covers them; the young (larvae) live in the water.
An Aedes mosquito takes 7 to 10 days to develop from an egg into an adult.
Aedes eggs can survive drying out for up to 8 months.
WHO links the spread of dengue to rising temperatures, heavy rainfall and high humidity; temperature also affects how quickly the virus develops inside the mosquito.
In early August 2015, heavy rain from Typhoon Soudelor increased the number of places where water collected in Taiwan, at a time when dengue cases were rising quickly in southern Taiwan.
Local cases are people who caught dengue inside Taiwan; cases caught abroad are counted separately as imported cases.
Taiwan had 43,419 local dengue cases in 2015 (by date of illness), the highest yearly total from 2010 to 2025. The 2014 total was 15,492 and the 2023 total was 26,429.
Of the 43,419 local cases in 2015, 22,760 were people living in Tainan and 19,723 were people living in Kaohsiung, together 42,483 cases, or about 98% of the total.
In 2016 local cases fell to 381, a few hundred, after the 43,419 cases of 2015. In 2021 there were no local cases at all.
Of the 26,429 local cases in 2023, 21,513 were people living in Tainan.
A vector expert told Taiwan CDC in 2015 that removing mosquito breeding sites is the single most effective way to control a dengue outbreak.
Health officials advise checking once a week and emptying and scrubbing, turning over, covering or throwing out anything that holds water; emptying and scrubbing removes mosquito eggs and larvae.
In 2015, local cases (by month of illness) rose from 335 in July to 4,461 in August and 15,166 in September.
